definition: Endogenous means caused by factors from within a system rather than from outside it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word endogenous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know endogenous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Biologists concluded the fishery's crash was endogenous, driven by the population's own overcrowding rather than by anything in the water flowing in.
Internal simply locates something inside, while endogenous makes a stronger claim: that a change was actually generated by the system's own workings.
An endogenous problem develops from within a system over time, but an innate trait is stronger still, built into a thing's very nature from the start.

Self-generated means produced by the thing itself — self-generated momentum, self-generated funding. Endogenous is the scholarly cousin that analysts use for causes arising inside the system under study, especially when weighing them against outside explanations. A team's energy is self-generated; an economic slowdown is endogenous.

Homegrown means developed from within, and it is informal with a warm, local flavor — homegrown talent, a homegrown solution. Endogenous is the technical term for the same inward origin, used when scientists or economists must classify a cause precisely. A festival celebrates homegrown music; a report labels a crisis endogenous.

A once-beloved restaurant began losing customers, and the owners first blamed a new food hall across town.

An outside consultant found something different: the kitchen had quietly cut portions, veteran servers had left after scheduling disputes, and reviews had complained about cold food long before the food hall ever opened.
The decline was endogenous, growing from problems inside the restaurant itself rather than from any rival outside it.
The restaurant's troubles arose from within its own operation, not from an outside competitor, which is what endogenous means.

When the city's deficit widened for the third straight year, the mayor blamed the state: aid had been trimmed, and the recession had not helped.
The auditors who arrived in March took nothing on faith and built the budget back from its own arithmetic.
Their conclusion was blunt: the shortfall was endogenous, produced by the city's own pension formula, which raised payouts automatically faster than revenue could ever grow.
State aid, they noted, had actually recovered two years earlier; the gap kept widening anyway.
The distinction mattered, the report argued, since a wound from outside might heal on its own, but a system that manufactures its own deficit will run one in good times and bad alike.
